book.title: Korkusuzluk (Feel the Fear and Do It Anyway)
book.author: Susan Jeffers

confidence_note: The concept is well attested: Jeffers devotes a chapter to moving from a victim stance to taking responsibility, defines responsibility as neither blaming others nor blaming yourself, and offers a 'Pain-to-Power Vocabulary' of word swaps. The specific exercise in the existing TR text (writing 'I chose this' under every complaint, with the job/relationship/money examples) could not be attributed to the book and is excluded. The TR claim that circumstances begin to change as attitude changes is not kept as a factual promise. Only the vocabulary pairs I am confident about are listed; the book's full list is longer.
facts: Jeffers argues that much fear is sustained by a 'victim' stance, in which what happens to us is someone or something else's doing.
She defines taking responsibility as never blaming anyone else for what you are being, doing, having or feeling, and also never blaming yourself.
In her framing, responsibility is about reclaiming power, not accepting guilt: blaming yourself is simply another way of staying a victim.

Her concrete tool is the 'Pain-to-Power Vocabulary', a set of word swaps: 'I can't' becomes 'I won't', 'I should' becomes 'I could', 'It's a problem' becomes 'It's an opportunity', 'It's not my fault' becomes 'I'm totally responsible', and 'It's terrible' becomes 'It's a learning experience'.
Jeffers' point is that the words we use shape how powerless or capable we feel about the same situation.
tension: Taking full responsibility sounds like signing up for blame. Jeffers insists that blaming yourself is exactly as disempowering as blaming others.
opening_idea: Start with a single phrase most people say several times a day, 'I can't', and Jeffers' suggestion to replace it with 'I won't', then ask what changes.

lessons.idea: Responsibility is the opposite of blame in both directions: not pointing at others, and not punishing yourself.
lessons.anchor: Jeffers' definition: never blaming anyone else, and never blaming yourself

lessons.idea: Swapping a single word can reveal a choice that the old word was hiding.
lessons.anchor: 'I can't' becomes 'I won't'; 'I should' becomes 'I could'

lessons.idea: Naming a setback as a learning experience keeps it from becoming a verdict on you.

reflect: When you say 'I can't' about something, how often would 'I won't' be the more honest sentence?
Do you tend to blame circumstances, other people, or yourself when something goes wrong?
reflect_final: The next time you hear yourself say 'I can't' or 'I should', try saying the Jeffers swap out loud and notice whether it reveals a choice you actually want to make, or one you want to decline.

use_cases.situation: In a meeting, someone says a task 'can't' be done this sprint.
use_cases.move: Ask gently: 'Is it can't, or won't given our other priorities?' then decide openly which item to drop.

use_cases.situation: You catch yourself saying 'I should call my parents more.'
use_cases.move: Jeffers' swap turns 'should' into 'could', so rephrase it as 'I could call them on Sunday' and decide whether you will.

use_cases.situation: A plan of yours fell apart and you are replaying whose fault it was.
use_cases.move: Write one line naming what you will do differently next time, without assigning blame to anyone, including yourself.

pocket_idea: 'I can't' often means 'I won't'. Say the honest word, and the choice becomes yours again.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Jeffers says blaming yourself is just another way of being a victim.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Susan Jeffers noticed how our words keep us powerless, so she offered a swap list: 'I can't' becomes 'I won't', 'I should' becomes 'I could', 'It's terrible' becomes 'It's a learning experience'. Responsibility, she says, means no blame in either direction.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What's something you say you 'can't' do that is really something you've decided not to do?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: Things that happen to me versus choices I am making about them.
